questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes greedy decoding from beam search in autoregressive language models?
questions.choice_A: Greedy decoding selects the single highest-probability token at each step, while beam search maintains multiple partial hypotheses to explore a set of high-probability sequences.
questions.choice_B: Greedy decoding samples from the full distribution at each step, while beam search deterministically selects the top token only.
questions.choice_C: Greedy decoding is stochastic, while beam search is always deterministic.
questions.choice_D: Greedy decoding guarantees the globally optimal sequence, while beam search is heuristic.

questions.question: In softmax with temperature $T$, $p_i \propto \exp(z_i/T)$, which qualitative effect does increasing $T$ typically have on the output distribution?
questions.choice_A: It sharpens the distribution, reducing entropy and diversity.
questions.choice_B: It flattens the distribution, increasing entropy and encouraging exploration.
questions.choice_C: It leaves the distribution unchanged but rescales logits for numerical stability only.
questions.choice_D: It forces probabilities to be uniform regardless of the logits.

questions.question: What is a key difference between top-k sampling and nucleus (top-p) sampling?
questions.choice_A: Top-k always chooses the top token, while top-p always samples uniformly.
questions.choice_B: Top-k fixes the candidate set size, while top-p adapts the set size to cover a target cumulative probability mass.
questions.choice_C: Top-k is deterministic, while top-p is deterministic only when $p=1.0$.
questions.choice_D: Top-k requires temperature, while top-p does not allow temperature to be applied.

questions.question: Which outcome is most commonly associated with greedy decoding compared to stochastic strategies?
questions.choice_A: Higher diversity and novelty of continuations
questions.choice_B: Lower diversity and a tendency to produce generic or repetitive outputs
questions.choice_C: Higher uncertainty and more exploratory outputs
questions.choice_D: Guaranteed improvement in human-judged quality

questions.question: Why can beam search with a very large beam width sometimes degrade human-judged quality despite improving sequence log-probability?
questions.choice_A: It increases randomness too much, producing incoherent text.
questions.choice_B: It amplifies exposure bias during training.
questions.choice_C: It can over-optimize for likelihood, favoring safe, generic, or length-biased sequences that human evaluators find bland or unnatural.
questions.choice_D: It violates the autoregressive factorization of the model.

questions.question: Which statement about deterministic vs. stochastic decoding is most accurate for open-ended generation?
questions.choice_A: Deterministic decoding guarantees factual correctness.
questions.choice_B: Stochastic decoding can improve diversity and creativity but may increase variance in quality.
questions.choice_C: Deterministic decoding always yields the maximum expected reward under any sequence-level metric.
questions.choice_D: Stochastic decoding is always preferable for exact reproduction tasks.

questions.question: How does temperature interact with top-k or top-p sampling in practice?
questions.choice_A: Temperature has no effect if top-k or top-p is used.
questions.choice_B: Temperature modifies relative probabilities within the truncated candidate set, allowing finer control of randomness.
questions.choice_C: Temperature only affects tokens outside the truncated set.
questions.choice_D: Temperature is equivalent to changing k or p by a constant factor.

questions.question: Which scenario best exemplifies the length bias problem in beam search?
questions.choice_A: Beam search always produces longer outputs because of temperature scaling.
questions.choice_B: Beam search prefers shorter sequences since multiplying probabilities across time reduces overall likelihood for longer outputs unless length normalization is used.
questions.choice_C: Beam search prefers longer outputs because cumulative probability mass increases with each token.
questions.choice_D: Beam search length bias is only present when k=1.

questions.question: What is the main idea behind best-of-N sampling as a selection strategy?
questions.choice_A: Generate N samples and average their token probabilities to produce a consensus output.
questions.choice_B: Generate N samples and pick the one with the highest sequence log-likelihood under the same model.
questions.choice_C: Generate N samples and select the best according to an external criterion (e.g., a reward model or a human-preferred metric).
questions.choice_D: Generate N samples and pick the one with the lowest entropy at each step.

questions.question: Which claim about top-p (nucleus) sampling is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: With very peaked distributions, top-p will often include many low-probability tokens.
questions.choice_B: With flat distributions, top-p increases the candidate set size to maintain the target cumulative probability, preserving flexibility.
questions.choice_C: Top-p always includes exactly k tokens.
questions.choice_D: Top-p forces uniform sampling over the included tokens regardless of temperature.

questions.question: In evaluating decoding strategies, why might sequence-level metrics like BLEU, ROUGE, or human preference differ from average token log-probability?
questions.choice_A: Token log-probability is invariant to decoding hyperparameters.
questions.choice_B: Sequence-level metrics capture global properties (content coverage, style, faithfulness) that are not fully reflected by local token likelihoods.
questions.choice_C: Sequence-level metrics are equivalent to token-level cross-entropy.
questions.choice_D: Token log-probability directly optimizes human judgments.

questions.question: Which adjustment is commonly used to mitigate beam search’s tendency toward short outputs?
questions.choice_A: Increase temperature
questions.choice_B: Length normalization or a length bonus in the beam scoring function
questions.choice_C: Decrease beam width to 1
questions.choice_D: Switch to greedy decoding

questions.question: What tradeoff typically arises when increasing beam width in conditional generation tasks like machine translation?
questions.choice_A: Higher diversity but lower coverage
questions.choice_B: Lower diversity but higher variance
questions.choice_C: Higher model likelihood and potential metric gains, but risk of generic or shorter outputs without proper normalization
questions.choice_D: No observable change if the model is well-trained

questions.question: Which description best characterizes the limit cases of temperature scaling?
questions.choice_A: $T \to 0$ approaches uniform sampling; $T \to \infty$ approaches argmax selection.
questions.choice_B: $T \to 0$ approaches argmax selection; $T \to \infty$ approaches uniform over the vocabulary.
questions.choice_C: $T \to 0$ and $T \to \infty$ both approach uniform sampling.
questions.choice_D: $T$ has no meaningful limit behavior in softmax.

questions.question: Why might top-k sampling with a small k harm factuality or coherence in some contexts?
questions.choice_A: It always includes rare tokens, increasing noise.
questions.choice_B: It may exclude necessary but moderately probable tokens, forcing choices from a too-narrow candidate set.
questions.choice_C: It removes the model's ability to use temperature scaling.
questions.choice_D: It makes the process deterministic and removes diversity.

questions.question: Which evaluation strategy aligns best with the goal of selecting the most helpful answer among multiple stochastic generations?
questions.choice_A: Choose the sample with the highest unigram entropy.
questions.choice_B: Choose the sample with the lowest average token rank.
questions.choice_C: Use best-of-N with a task-aligned reranker, such as a reward model or human preference model.
questions.choice_D: Always choose the shortest sample to minimize risk.

questions.question: What is a known risk when combining large beam widths with purely likelihood-based reranking in open-ended dialogue?
questions.choice_A: Systematic preference for highly specific, creative responses
questions.choice_B: Mode collapse to bland, high-likelihood replies and reduced conversational diversity
questions.choice_C: Explosion of contradictory statements across beams
questions.choice_D: Guaranteed grammatical errors due to low-entropy decisions

questions.question: How do decoding hyperparameters interact with sequence-level metrics during model development?
questions.choice_A: Once the model is trained, decoding hyperparameters do not affect any metric.
questions.choice_B: Metrics like BLEU/ROUGE or human preference can change substantially with temperature, k/p, and beam width, so tuning decoding is part of achieving reported performance.
questions.choice_C: Only perplexity is sensitive to decoding hyperparameters.
questions.choice_D: Changing decoding only affects runtime, not quality metrics.

questions.question: Which approach best balances diversity and quality when generating creative but coherent text?
questions.choice_A: Greedy decoding with $T=0$
questions.choice_B: High temperature with no truncation
questions.choice_C: Moderate temperature with top-p sampling and a small $p$ that adapts to context
questions.choice_D: Very large beam width with strong length penalty

questions.question: What is a practical consideration when using best-of-N sampling regarding computational budget?
questions.choice_A: It is computationally free because selection replaces generation.
questions.choice_B: Its cost scales roughly linearly with N due to generating multiple candidates, plus the cost of reranking.
questions.choice_C: Its cost is dominated by backpropagation through the model.
questions.choice_D: It requires training a larger base model to be effective.

questions.question: Which statement about entropy and observed diversity in generated sequences is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: Higher per-step entropy guarantees higher human-perceived diversity at the sequence level.
questions.choice_B: Lower per-step entropy always improves human preference.
questions.choice_C: Increasing entropy via temperature often increases diversity, but sequence-level diversity also depends on truncation schemes and long-range dependencies.
questions.choice_D: Entropy does not relate to diversity in language generation.
